questions.stem: Two point particles of mass $m_1 = 4.0\text{ kg}$ and $m_2 = 9.0\text{ kg}$ are separated by a center-to-center distance of $r = 3.0\text{ m}$ in empty space. Given the universal gravitational constant $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2$, what is the magnitude of the mutual gravitational attractive force between them?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Two isolated point masses in vacuum

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Applying Newton's universal inverse-square law F = G * m1 * m2 / r^2 with proper distance squaring.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires parameter substitution and quantitative arithmetic evaluation, not bare recall.

B.diagnostic: Forgot to square the separation distance r in the denominator: F = G * m1 * m2 / r = 8.00e-10 N.

C.diagnostic: Divided by r^3 instead of r^2 in the denominator: F = G * m1 * m2 / r^3 = 8.89e-11 N.

D.diagnostic: Multiplied by r^2 instead of dividing: F = G * m1 * m2 * r^2 = 2.40e-9 N.

progressive_hints.title: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation
progressive_hints.text: The mutual gravitational force between two point masses is given by $F = G \frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}$.

progressive_hints.title: Substitute Parameters
progressive_hints.text: Plug in $m_1 = 4.0\text{ kg}$, $m_2 = 9.0\text{ kg}$, $r = 3.0\text{ m}$, and $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2$. Notice that $r^2 = 9.0\text{ m}^2$ cancels directly with $m_2 = 9.0\text{ kg}$.

derivation_steps: State Newton's gravitational formula: $F = G \frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}$.
Substitute numerical constants and variables: $F = (6.67 \times 10^{-11}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2) \frac{(4.0\text{ kg})(9.0\text{ kg})}{(3.0\text{ m})^2}$.
Simplify terms: $\frac{36.0}{9.0} = 4.0$.
Multiply: $F = 4.0 \times 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\text{ N} = 2.67 \times 10^{-10}\text{ N}$.

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: F -> 0 (gravitational attraction vanishes at asymptotic separation)
F -> 0 (zero mass yields zero gravitational interaction)

questions.stem: The Earth has mass $M_E \approx 5.97 \times 10^{24}\text{ kg}$ and an apple falling near Earth's surface has mass $m_a = 0.20\text{ kg}$. If the Earth exerts a downward gravitational force of magnitude $F_E = 1.96\text{ N}$ on the apple, what is the magnitude of the upward gravitational force $F_a$ exerted by the apple on the Earth?

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Recognizing that Newton's third law requires gravitational action-reaction forces to be strictly equal in magnitude regardless of mass disparity.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires no algebraic calculation; relies on fundamental Third Law invariance.

A.diagnostic: By Newton's Third Law, gravitational interaction forms an action-reaction pair: F_apple_on_Earth = F_Earth_on_apple = 1.96 N exactly.

B.diagnostic: Scaled force down by the mass ratio m_a / M_E, assuming a lighter body exerts a proportionately smaller force.

C.diagnostic: Scaled force up by Earth's mass M_E, confusing force with planetary mass.

D.diagnostic: Assumed small objects cannot exert any gravitational force on a massive planet.

progressive_hints.title: Newton's Third Law of Motion
progressive_hints.text: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction. If object 1 exerts force $\vec{F}_{12}$ on object 2, then object 2 exerts force $\vec{F}_{21} = -\vec{F}_{12}$ on object 1.

progressive_hints.title: Universal Gravitation Symmetry
progressive_hints.text: The gravitational force magnitude is $F = G \frac{M_E m_a}{r^2}$. Both masses enter this formula symmetrically as a product $M_E m_a$.

progressive_hints.title: Conclusion
progressive_hints.text: Because the product $M_E m_a$ is identical whether viewed from the Earth or the apple, the apple attracts the Earth with the exact same magnitude: $F_a = F_E = 1.96\text{ N}$.

derivation_steps: Gravitational force on the apple by Earth: $F_E = G \frac{M_E m_a}{R_E^2} = 1.96\text{ N}$.
Gravitational force on Earth by the apple: $F_a = G \frac{m_a M_E}{R_E^2}$.
By commutativity of multiplication, $M_E m_a = m_a M_E$, so $F_a = F_E = 1.96\text{ N}$.

questions.stem: From Newton's universal gravitational law $F = G \frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}$, what are the base SI dimensions of the universal gravitational constant $G$?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Dimensional equation for universal gravitational constant

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Isolating G = F * r^2 / (m1 * m2) and substituting base SI dimensions [M L T^-2] * [L^2] / [M^2].

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Direct dimensional formula derivation from primitive base dimensions.

A.diagnostic: Correctly derived [G] = [F][r^2]/[m^2] = [M L T^-2][L^2]/[M^2] = [M^-1 L^3 T^-2].

B.diagnostic: Incorrectly assigned positive exponent to mass: [M L^3 T^-2].

C.diagnostic: Used [L^2] instead of [L^3] for length dimension: [M^-1 L^2 T^-2].

D.diagnostic: Confused dimensions of G with angular momentum [M L^2 T^-1].

progressive_hints.title: Rearrange for G
progressive_hints.text: Isolate $G$ from $F = G \frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}$: $G = \frac{F r^2}{m_1 m_2}$.

progressive_hints.title: Insert SI Base Dimensions
progressive_hints.text: Force has dimensions $[F] = [M L T^{-2}]$, distance squared $[r^2] = [L^2]$, and mass squared $[m_1 m_2] = [M^2]$.

derivation_steps: Formula: $G = \frac{F r^2}{m_1 m_2}$.
Dimensional breakdown: $[F] = M L T^{-2}$, $[r^2] = L^2$, $[m_1 m_2] = M^2$.

questions.stem: An exoplanet has twice the mass of Earth ($M_p = 2 M_E$) and twice the radius of Earth ($R_p = 2 R_E$). If the acceleration due to gravity at Earth's surface is $g_E = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$, what is the acceleration due to gravity $g_p$ at the surface of this exoplanet?

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Applying surface gravity formula g = GM / R^2 and scaling by (M_p / M_E) / (R_p / R_E)^2 = 2 / 2^2 = 1/2.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires proportional algebraic ratio scaling, not direct recall.

A.diagnostic: Correctly determined g_p = G (2 M_E) / (2 R_E)^2 = (2 / 4) * (G M_E / R_E^2) = 0.5 * 9.8 = 4.9 m/s^2.

B.diagnostic: Assumed g scales linearly with radius: 2 / 2 = 1, giving 9.8 m/s^2.

C.diagnostic: Multiplied by mass factor 2 without dividing by radius squared: 2 * 9.8 = 19.6 m/s^2.

D.diagnostic: Divided by 2^2 = 4 without multiplying by the mass factor of 2: 9.8 / 4 = 2.45 m/s^2.

progressive_hints.title: Surface Gravity Formula
progressive_hints.text: Surface gravity is given by $g = \frac{GM}{R^2}$.

progressive_hints.title: Set Up Ratio
progressive_hints.text: For the exoplanet, $\frac{g_p}{g_E} = \frac{M_p}{M_E} \times \left(\frac{R_E}{R_p}\right)^2$.

progressive_hints.title: Substitute Ratios
progressive_hints.text: With $M_p / M_E = 2$ and $R_p / R_E = 2$, $\frac{g_p}{g_E} = 2 \times \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{2}{4} = \frac{1}{2}$, so $g_p = \frac{9.8}{2} = 4.9\text{ m/s}^2$.

derivation_steps: Earth surface gravity: $g_E = \frac{G M_E}{R_E^2}$.
Exoplanet surface gravity: $g_p = \frac{G M_p}{R_p^2} = \frac{G (2 M_E)}{(2 R_E)^2} = \frac{2}{4} \frac{G M_E}{R_E^2} = \frac{1}{2} g_E$.
Evaluate: $g_p = 0.5 \times 9.8\text{ m/s}^2 = 4.9\text{ m/s}^2$.

questions.stem: Assuming the Earth is a uniform solid sphere of radius $R_E$ and surface gravity $g_0$, at what depth $d$ below the Earth's surface does the acceleration due to gravity equal $25\%$ of its surface value ($g = 0.25 g_0$)?

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Applying Newton's Shell Theorem to establish linear field scaling g(r) = g_0 * (r/R_E) and converting distance from center r = 0.25 R_E into depth from surface d = R_E - r = 0.75 R_E.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires shell theorem integration and distinguishing depth from radial distance.

A.diagnostic: Inside a uniform sphere, g(d) = g_0 (1 - d/R_E). Setting g = 0.25 g_0 gives 1 - d/R_E = 0.25, so d = 0.75 R_E.

B.diagnostic: Confused depth from surface d with distance from center r = 0.25 R_E.

C.diagnostic: Assumed gravity decreases as square root of depth, giving d = 0.50 R_E.

D.diagnostic: Mistakenly applied exterior inverse-square law inside Earth: 1/r^2 = 0.25 => r = 2 R_E, d = 0.87 R_E.

progressive_hints.title: Shell Theorem Inside a Solid Sphere
progressive_hints.text: By Newton's shell theorem, all outer shells exert zero net force. The enclosed mass is $M(r) = M_E (r/R_E)^3$.

progressive_hints.title: Linear Variation with Depth
progressive_hints.text: The field at radial distance $r = R_E - d$ is $g(d) = g_0 \frac{r}{R_E} = g_0 \left(1 - \frac{d}{R_E}\right)$.

progressive_hints.title: Solve for Depth d
progressive_hints.text: Set $g(d) = 0.25 g_0$: $1 - \frac{d}{R_E} = 0.25 \implies \frac{d}{R_E} = 1 - 0.25 = 0.75 \implies d = 0.75 R_E$.

derivation_steps: Gravitational field at distance $r \le R_E$ from center: $g(r) = \frac{G M(r)}{r^2} = \frac{G (M_E r^3 / R_E^3)}{r^2} = \frac{G M_E}{R_E^3} r = g_0 \frac{r}{R_E}$.
Depth $d$ is defined as $d = R_E - r$, so $r = R_E - d$.
Substitute: $g(d) = g_0 \left(\frac{R_E - d}{R_E}\right) = g_0 \left(1 - \frac{d}{R_E}\right)$.
Set $g(d) = 0.25 g_0 \implies 1 - \frac{d}{R_E} = 0.25 \implies d = 0.75 R_E$.

questions.stem: At what altitude $h$ above the Earth's surface does the acceleration due to gravity decrease to $\frac{1}{4}$ of its surface value $g_0$ (in terms of Earth's radius $R_E$)?

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Using exact inverse-square variation g(h) = g_0 * (R_E / (R_E + h))^2 = 1/4 rather than linear approximation.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires algebraic quadratic solving and recognizing scope limits of approximations.

A.diagnostic: Correctly solved (R_E / (R_E + h))^2 = 1/4 => R_E / (R_E + h) = 1/2 => R_E + h = 2 R_E => h = R_E.

B.diagnostic: Confused radial distance r = 2 R_E with altitude above surface h = r - R_E = R_E.

C.diagnostic: Took square root of 1/4 as 1/2 and set h/R_E = 1/2 => h = 0.5 R_E.

D.diagnostic: Erroneously used small-altitude approximation 1 - 2h/R_E = 0.25 => 2h/R_E = 0.75 => h = 0.375 R_E.

progressive_hints.title: Exact Altitude Formula
progressive_hints.text: At height $h$, radial distance is $r = R_E + h$. The exact acceleration is $g(h) = \frac{GM_E}{(R_E + h)^2} = g_0 \left(\frac{R_E}{R_E + h}\right)^2$.

progressive_hints.title: Avoid Small-Angle Approximations
progressive_hints.text: Because the change is large ($75\%$ decrease), the binomial approximation $g \approx g_0(1 - 2h/R)$ fails completely. Use the exact formula.

progressive_hints.title: Take Square Root
progressive_hints.text: $\left(\frac{R_E}{R_E + h}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4} \implies \frac{R_E}{R_E + h} = \frac{1}{2} \implies R_E + h = 2 R_E \implies h = R_E$.

derivation_steps: Exact expression: $g(h) = g_0 \frac{R_E^2}{(R_E + h)^2}$.
Equate to target value: $g_0 \frac{R_E^2}{(R_E + h)^2} = \frac{1}{4} g_0$.
Cancel $g_0$ and take square root: $\frac{R_E}{R_E + h} = \frac{1}{2}$.
Cross-multiply: $2 R_E = R_E + h \implies h = R_E$.

questions.stem: A comet orbits the Sun in an eccentric elliptical orbit. Its closest distance to the Sun (perihelion) is $r_p = 0.50\text{ AU}$ and its farthest distance (aphelion) is $r_a = 4.50\text{ AU}$. If the comet's linear orbital speed at perihelion is $v_p = 54.0\text{ km/s}$, what is its linear orbital speed $v_a$ at aphelion?

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Applying conservation of angular momentum under central force at apsides: m * r_p * v_p = m * r_a * v_a.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires setting up conservation equation and calculating reciprocal speed ratio.

A.diagnostic: At apsides, velocity is perpendicular to radius vector. Conservation of angular momentum gives v_a = v_p (r_p / r_a) = 54.0 * (0.50 / 4.50) = 54.0 / 9 = 6.0 km/s.

B.diagnostic: Assumed planetary speed is uniform along an elliptical orbit.

C.diagnostic: Inverted distance ratio: v_a = v_p * (r_a / r_p) = 54.0 * 9 = 486 km/s.

D.diagnostic: Divided by 3 instead of 9: 54 / 3 = 18.0 km/s.

progressive_hints.title: Central Force Torque Invariant
progressive_hints.text: Because the gravitational force points toward the Sun, net torque about the Sun is zero: $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F} = \vec{0}$, so angular momentum $\vec{L}$ is conserved.

progressive_hints.title: Speed-Distance Reciprocity at Apsides
progressive_hints.text: At perihelion and aphelion, the velocity is strictly perpendicular to the position vector: $L = m r_p v_p = m r_a v_a$.

derivation_steps: Angular momentum definition: $\vec{L} = \vec{r} \times (m\vec{v})$.
Torque equation: $\frac{d\vec{L}}{dt} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}_g = \vec{0} \implies \vec{L} = \text{constant}$.
At perihelion and aphelion, $\vec{r} \perp \vec{v}$, so $L_p = m r_p v_p$ and $L_a = m r_a v_a$.
Equate: $m r_p v_p = m r_a v_a \implies v_a = v_p \frac{r_p}{r_a}$.
Substitute values: $v_a = 54.0\text{ km/s} \times \frac{0.50\text{ AU}}{4.50\text{ AU}} = 6.0\text{ km/s}$.

questions.stem: Satellite $A$ moves in a circular orbit of radius $r_A = R$ around a planet with an orbital period of $T_A = 8.0\text{ hours}$. Satellite $B$ orbits the same planet in a circular orbit of radius $r_B = 4.0 R$. What is the orbital period $T_B$ of Satellite $B$?

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Applying Kepler's third law ratio T_B / T_A = (r_B / r_A)^(3/2) = 4^(1.5) = 8.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires applying power 3/2 scaling, not bare recall of statement.

A.diagnostic: By Kepler's Third Law, T^2 ∝ r^3 => T_B = T_A * (r_B / r_A)^(3/2) = 8.0 * 4^(3/2) = 8.0 * 8 = 64.0 hours.

B.diagnostic: Assumed linear period scaling T ∝ r: T_B = 8.0 * 4 = 32.0 hours.

C.diagnostic: Took square root instead of 3/2 power: 8.0 * sqrt(4) = 16.0 hours.

D.diagnostic: Scaled by r^2 instead of r^(3/2): 8.0 * 4^2 = 128.0 hours.

progressive_hints.title: Kepler's Third Law Formula
progressive_hints.text: For circular orbits under gravity, centripetal force equals gravitational force: $m \frac{4\pi^2 r}{T^2} = \frac{GMm}{r^2} \implies T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM} r^3$.

progressive_hints.title: Set Up Ratio

progressive_hints.text: For $h \ll R_E$, $g(h) \approx g_0 \left(1 - \frac{2h}{R_E}\right)$, so $\frac{\Delta g_h}{g_0} = \frac{2h}{R_E}$.

progressive_hints.title: Fractional Decrease with Depth
progressive_hints.text: For depth $d$, $g(d) = g_0 \left(1 - \frac{d}{R_E}\right)$, so $\frac{\Delta g_d}{g_0} = \frac{d}{R_E}$.

progressive_hints.title: Equate and Solve
progressive_hints.text: $\frac{2h}{R_E} = \frac{d}{R_E} \implies 2h = d \implies h = \frac{d}{2} = \frac{10.0\text{ km}}{2} = 5.0\text{ km}$.

derivation_steps: Altitude variation: $g(h) = g_0 (1 + h/R_E)^{-2} \approx g_0 (1 - 2h/R_E) \implies \Delta g_h = g_0 \frac{2h}{R_E}$.
Depth variation: $g(d) = g_0 (1 - d/R_E) \implies \Delta g_d = g_0 \frac{d}{R_E}$.
Equating fractional changes: $\frac{2h}{R_E} = \frac{d}{R_E}$.
Solve for $h$: $h = \frac{d}{2} = \frac{10.0\text{ km}}{2} = 5.0\text{ km}$.

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Modeling restoring force F(x) = -(mg_0/R_E)*x as SHM with period T = 2*pi*sqrt(R_E/g_0) and computing one-way transit time t = T/2.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires proving SHM equivalence from Gauss's law / shell theorem before evaluating transit time.

A.diagnostic: SHM period T = 2*pi*sqrt(R_E/g_0) = 2*pi*sqrt(6.4e6/9.8) = 5077 s = 84.6 min. One-way transit is half an oscillation: t = T/2 = 42.3 min.

B.diagnostic: Reported the full round-trip oscillation period T = 84.6 min instead of the one-way transit time.

C.diagnostic: Reported time to fall to center (quarter period T/4 = 21.1 min) instead of traversing the entire planet.

D.diagnostic: Assumed constant acceleration under surface gravity g_0: t = sqrt(2 * 2R_E / g_0) = 59.8 min.

progressive_hints.title: Restoring Force Inside Earth
progressive_hints.text: By the shell theorem, at distance $x$ from the center, $F(x) = -\frac{G M(x) m}{x^2} = -\frac{G M_E m}{R_E^3} x = -\frac{m g_0}{R_E} x$. This is Hooke's Law $F = -k x$!

progressive_hints.title: Simple Harmonic Motion Frequency & Period
progressive_hints.text: The effective spring constant is $k = \frac{m g_0}{R_E}$. Angular frequency is $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{g_0}{R_E}}$. The full period is $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{R_E}{g_0}}$.

progressive_hints.title: Compute One-Way Transit Time
progressive_hints.text: The ball oscillates between $x = +R_E$ and $x = -R_E$. Going from surface to opposite surface is half a period: $t_{\text{transit}} = \frac{T}{2} = \pi \sqrt{\frac{R_E}{g_0}} = \pi \sqrt{\frac{6.40 \times 10^6}{9.80}} = 2539\text{ s} \approx 42.3\text{ minutes}$.

derivation_steps: Restoring force at radial position $x$: $F(x) = -\frac{G (M_E x^3 / R_E^3) m}{x^2} = -\left(\frac{m g_0}{R_E}\right) x$.
Equation of motion: $m \frac{d^2 x}{dt^2} = -\left(\frac{m g_0}{R_E}\right) x \implies \frac{d^2 x}{dt^2} + \left(\frac{g_0}{R_E}\right) x = 0$.
This is SHM with $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{g_0}{R_E}}$.
Period of full oscillation: $T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{R_E}{g_0}} \approx 5077\text{ s} \approx 84.6\text{ minutes}$.
One-way transit from $+R_E$ to $-R_E$ is half a period: $t = \frac{T}{2} = \pi \sqrt{\frac{R_E}{g_0}} \approx 2539\text{ s} \approx 42.3\text{ minutes}$.

system_parameters.system_boundary: Earth ocean envelope under lunar differential gravity

options.A: $a_{\text{tide}} \propto \frac{1}{d^3}$; near ocean is pulled toward Moon faster than solid Earth, while solid Earth is pulled faster than far ocean
options.B: $a_{\text{tide}} \propto \frac{1}{d^2}$; Moon attracts ocean water only on the near side of Earth

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires derivative calculus on inverse-square field and relative frame transformation.

A.diagnostic: a_tide = g(near) - g(center) ≈ (dg/dd) * R_E = 2 G M_M R_E / d^3 ∝ 1/d^3. Subtracting the common acceleration of Earth center leaves outward differential forces on BOTH near side and far side.

C.diagnostic: Assumed inverse-fourth power scaling.

D.diagnostic: Assumed inverse-linear scaling and attributed tides primarily to Coriolis forces.

progressive_hints.title: Tides as a Differential Force
progressive_hints.text: Tides are not caused by the absolute pull of the Moon, but by the DIFFERENCE in the Moon's pull across the diameter of Earth.

progressive_hints.title: Derivative of Gravitational Field
progressive_hints.text: Gravitational field is $g(d) = \frac{GM_M}{d^2}$. The gradient is $\left|\frac{dg}{dd}\right| = \frac{2GM_M}{d^3}$. Across radius $R_E$, $\Delta g \approx \frac{2GM_M R_E}{d^3} \propto \frac{1}{d^3}$.

progressive_hints.title: Why Two Bulges?
progressive_hints.text: In Earth's free-falling frame, subtract the acceleration of Earth's center: the near side accelerates toward the Moon relative to Earth (bulge 1), and Earth accelerates away from the far side, leaving the far water behind (bulge 2)!

derivation_steps: Gravitational acceleration at Earth center: $g_0 = \frac{G M_M}{d^2}$.
Gravitational acceleration at sub-lunar near point ($d - R_E$): $g_{\text{near}} = \frac{G M_M}{(d - R_E)^2} \approx \frac{G M_M}{d^2} \left(1 + \frac{2R_E}{d}\right)$.
Differential tidal acceleration: $a_{\text{tide}} = g_{\text{near}} - g_0 \approx \frac{2 G M_M R_E}{d^3} \propto \frac{1}{d^3}$.

At the anti-lunar far point ($d + R_E$): $g_{\text{far}} \approx \frac{G M_M}{d^2} \left(1 - \frac{2R_E}{d}\right) \implies g_{\text{far}} - g_0 \approx -\frac{2 G M_M R_E}{d^3}$, directed away from Earth's center.
This produces two equal and opposite tidal bulges.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires piecewise line integral of electric/gravitational potential from infinity through interior.

A.diagnostic: V(R) = -GM/R. Inside, g(r) = (GM/R^3)*r. V_c - V(R) = -int_R^0 (GM/R^3) r dr = (GM/R^3) [r^2 / 2]_0^R = GM / (2R). Thus V_c = -GM/R - GM/(2R) = -1.5 GM/R.

C.diagnostic: Conflated gravitational field (which is zero at center: g = 0) with gravitational potential.

progressive_hints.text: From infinity to surface, the planet behaves as a point mass: $V(R) = -\frac{GM}{R}$.

progressive_hints.title: Field Inside Planet
progressive_hints.text: Inside the planet ($r \le R$), the field points inward: $\vec{g}(r) = -\frac{GM}{R^3} r \hat{r}$.

progressive_hints.title: Line Integral to Center
progressive_hints.text: Potential difference: $V_c - V(R) = -\int_R^0 \left(-\frac{GM}{R^3} r\right) dr = \frac{GM}{R^3} \left[\frac{r^2}{2}\right]_0^R = -\frac{GM}{2R}$. Thus $V_c = V(R) - \frac{GM}{2R} = -\frac{GM}{R} - \frac{GM}{2R} = -\frac{3}{2}\frac{GM}{R}$.

derivation_steps: Potential at surface: $V(R) = -\int_\infty^R \vec{g} \cdot d\vec{r} = -\frac{GM}{R}$.
Work done moving a unit mass from $R$ to $0$: $V(0) - V(R) = -\int_R^0 g(r) dr$.
Since $g(r) = \frac{GM}{R^3} r$: $\int_R^0 \frac{GM}{R^3} r dr = \frac{GM}{R^3} \left[\frac{r^2}{2}\right]_R^0 = -\frac{GM}{2R}$.

Correct step: $V(0) = V(R) - \int_0^R g(r) dr = -\frac{GM}{R} - \frac{GM}{2R} = -\frac{3}{2} \frac{GM}{R}$.

questions.stem: A solid sphere of uniform mass density $\rho$ and radius $R$ has an off-center spherical cavity of radius $R_c = R/3$ scooped out of it. The center of the cavity is displaced from the center of the large sphere by vector $\vec{d}$. Using the principle of superposition, what is the gravitational field $\vec{g}_{\text{cav}}$ at ANY point inside the cavity?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Perforated solid sphere with off-center hollow cavity
system_parameters.reference_frame: Origin at center of main sphere

options.C: $\vec{g}_{\text{cav}} = -\frac{4}{3} \pi G \rho \vec{r}$ (varies linearly with distance from main center)
options.D: $\vec{g}_{\text{cav}} = -\frac{4}{3} \pi G \rho (\vec{r} - \vec{d})$ (varies linearly with distance from cavity center)

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Applying superposition g_cav = g_solid - g_cavity_mass and showing that position vector r cancels identically, leaving a uniform field proportional to displacement vector d.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires vector superposition proof demonstrating surprising uniformity of the cavity field.

A.diagnostic: g_cav = g_full(r) - g_scoop(r - d) = -4/3 pi G rho r - (-4/3 pi G rho (r - d)) = -4/3 pi G rho d. The field is completely independent of r and strictly uniform everywhere inside the cavity!

B.diagnostic: Misapplied shell theorem, incorrectly assuming cavity field must vanish like a concentric shell.

C.diagnostic: Neglected the negative mass subtraction of the scooped cavity.

D.diagnostic: Assumed field depends purely on displacement from cavity center.

progressive_hints.title: Superposition Principle
progressive_hints.text: The cavity can be represented as a full solid sphere of positive density $+\rho$ plus a smaller sphere of negative density $-\rho$ located at the cavity position.

progressive_hints.title: Vector Field Inside a Solid Sphere
progressive_hints.text: Inside a solid sphere centered at origin: $\vec{g}_1(\vec{r}) = -\frac{4}{3} \pi G \rho \vec{r}$. For a sphere centered at $\vec{d}$, the field at $\vec{r}$ is $\vec{g}_2(\vec{r}) = -\frac{4}{3} \pi G (-\rho) (\vec{r} - \vec{d}) = +\frac{4}{3} \pi G \rho (\vec{r} - \vec{d})$.

progressive_hints.title: Add the Two Fields
progressive_hints.text: $\vec{g}_{\text{cav}} = \vec{g}_1 + \vec{g}_2 = -\frac{4}{3} \pi G \rho \vec{r} + \frac{4}{3} \pi G \rho \vec{r} - \frac{4}{3} \pi G \rho \vec{d} = -\frac{4}{3} \pi G \rho \vec{d}$. The position vector $\vec{r}$ cancels completely!

derivation_steps: Consider point $P$ inside the cavity with position vector $\vec{r}$ relative to center $O_1$ of the large sphere.
Field due to complete solid sphere: $\vec{g}_{\text{full}} = -\frac{G M(r)}{r^2} \hat{r} = -\frac{4}{3} \pi G \rho \vec{r}$.
The scooped region has center at $\vec{d}$. The position of $P$ relative to cavity center $O_2$ is $\vec{r}' = \vec{r} - \vec{d}$.
Field exerted by the removed mass of density $\rho$: $\vec{g}_{\text{rem}} = -\frac{4}{3} \pi G \rho (\vec{r} - \vec{d})$.

By superposition: $\vec{g}_{\text{cav}} = \vec{g}_{\text{full}} - \vec{g}_{\text{rem}} = -\frac{4}{3} \pi G \rho \vec{r} - \left[-\frac{4}{3} \pi G \rho (\vec{r} - \vec{d})\right] = -\frac{4}{3} \pi G \rho \vec{d}$.
This proves $\vec{g}_{\text{cav}}$ is constant in magnitude and direction everywhere in the cavity.

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: g_cav -> 0 (recovers Shell Theorem spherical shell interior null field)
Field points opposite to displacement vector d (toward the heavier side where more mass remains)

questions.stem: A space probe is launched vertically upward from the surface of Earth ($R_E = 6400\text{ km}$, surface escape velocity $v_{\text{esc}} = 11.2\text{ km/s}$) with an initial launch speed $v_0 = 3.0 v_{\text{esc}} = 33.6\text{ km/s}$. Neglecting atmospheric drag and Earth's rotation, what is the probe's residual speed $v_\infty$ as it escapes to an infinite distance from Earth?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Unbound probe in Earth's gravitational potential well

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Applying conservation of mechanical energy: 0.5*m*v_0^2 - GMm/R = 0.5*m*v_inf^2 => v_inf = sqrt(v_0^2 - v_esc^2) = sqrt(9 - 1)*v_esc = sqrt(8)*v_esc = 2*sqrt(2)*v_esc.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires hyperbolic trajectory energy analysis and non-linear kinetic difference derivation.

A.diagnostic: By conservation of energy: E = 0.5 m v0^2 - GMm/R = 0.5 m v_inf^2. Since v_esc^2 = 2GM/R, v_inf^2 = v0^2 - v_esc^2 = (3 v_esc)^2 - v_esc^2 = 8 v_esc^2 => v_inf = sqrt(8) v_esc = 2.828 * 11.2 km/s = 31.68 km/s ≈ 31.7 km/s.

B.diagnostic: Subtracted speeds linearly: v_inf = v0 - v_esc = 3 v_esc - v_esc = 2 v_esc = 22.4 km/s, violating conservation of energy.

C.diagnostic: Assumed gravity does no net work on a high-speed body, so v_inf = v0 = 33.6 km/s.

D.diagnostic: Took square root of 3 instead of 8: sqrt(3) * 11.2 = 19.4 km/s.

progressive_hints.title: Conservation of Mechanical Energy
progressive_hints.text: Total energy at launch equals total energy at infinity: $E_{\text{launch}} = \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 - \frac{GMm}{R_E} = \frac{1}{2} m v_\infty^2 + 0$.

progressive_hints.title: Substitute Escape Velocity
progressive_hints.text: Since $v_{\text{esc}}^2 = \frac{2GM}{R_E}$, the potential energy term is $\frac{GMm}{R_E} = \frac{1}{2} m v_{\text{esc}}^2$. Thus $\frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 - \frac{1}{2} m v_{\text{esc}}^2 = \frac{1}{2} m v_\infty^2$.

progressive_hints.title: Solve for Asymptotic Speed
progressive_hints.text: $v_\infty = \sqrt{v_0^2 - v_{\text{esc}}^2} = \sqrt{(3 v_{\text{esc}})^2 - v_{\text{esc}}^2} = \sqrt{9 v_{\text{esc}}^2 - v_{\text{esc}}^2} = \sqrt{8} v_{\text{esc}} = 2\sqrt{2} v_{\text{esc}} \approx 2.828 \times 11.2\text{ km/s} \approx 31.7\text{ km/s}$.

derivation_steps: Total initial mechanical energy at planetary surface: $E_0 = \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 - \frac{G M_E m}{R_E}$.
Recall definition of escape speed: $\frac{1}{2} m v_{\text{esc}}^2 - \frac{G M_E m}{R_E} = 0 \implies \frac{G M_E m}{R_E} = \frac{1}{2} m v_{\text{esc}}^2$.
Substitute into initial energy: $E_0 = \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 - \frac{1}{2} m v_{\text{esc}}^2 = \frac{1}{2} m (v_0^2 - v_{\text{esc}}^2)$.
At $r \to \infty$, gravitational potential energy vanishes ($U(\infty) = 0$), so $E_\infty = \frac{1}{2} m v_\infty^2$.
Equating energies: $\frac{1}{2} m v_\infty^2 = \frac{1}{2} m (v_0^2 - v_{\text{esc}}^2) \implies v_\infty = \sqrt{v_0^2 - v_{\text{esc}}^2}$.
Substitute $v_0 = 3 v_{\text{esc}}$: $v_\infty = \sqrt{9 v_{\text{esc}}^2 - v_{\text{esc}}^2} = \sqrt{8} v_{\text{esc}} = 2\sqrt{2} v_{\text{esc}} \approx 31.68\text{ km/s} \approx 31.7\text{ km/s}$.

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: v_inf = sqrt(v_esc^2 - v_esc^2) = 0 (exact threshold of escape)
v_inf approx v_0 * (1 - 0.5 * (v_esc/v_0)^2) -> v_0 (gravitational well becomes negligible)
